utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Let's have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleague Ms. McHenry and Mr. Huber for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Edina Residovic, I appear for the defence of Mr. Zejnil Delalic together with my colleague Eugene O'Sullivan professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Helen Buturovic from Konjic from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'm the attorney of Mr. Mucic. Together with me is my colleague, Mr. Kuzmanovic, an attorney from America, and Mr. Niko Duric, the attorney from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Salih Karabdic, I'm a lawyer from Sarajevo and I represent the defence of Mr. Delic. Together with me is my colleague from Houston, Texas, Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Cynthia McMurrey and along with my colleagues Ms. Nancy Boler and Mr. Calvin Saunders, we represent Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, may we hear you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. By this stage of the proceeding, Your Honours have heard many thousands of words, and probably you've heard about as many words as you want to hear in relation to this case, so I promise that I will try and be as brief as I can be. But I would like, if I could, to attempt to destroy some of the myths that have been created in this case, and particularly in the submissions that have been made by my colleagues from the Defence. So, in doing that, I fear that I may well take the full extent of my half-hour, and I may indeed, if necessary, have to seek Your Honours' indulgence to borrow a little bit of time from that left over by my colleague, Mrs. McHenry, yesterday, who kindly completed her submissions in a timely fashion and leaves 15 minutes over for the Prosecution, if Your Honours would indulge me. I sincerely hope that is not necessary. So, Your Honours, there's been a number of factors, a number of issues that have been raised by the Defence which we, from this side of the courtroom, say are myths, are not true, not correct. The first one, Your Honours, that I'd like to deal with is in the submission by Mr. Delalic. There's a reference they, somewhat guarded, I might say, and perhaps equivocal, but nonetheless exists, which asserts that the Prosecution has the obligation to prove every fact in the indictment. Your Honours have no doubt seen that. Your Honours, the Prosecution must prove every fact in the indictment that goes to proof of an element of the offence. Indictments are not they merely to set out the facts which the Prosecution must prove and if one of those facts is not proved that's the end of the case. The position is, Your Honours, that indictments, as you well know, serve a number of purposes; they inform the accused of the circumstances of the case, they give particulars and they also set out the charges, and they should express those words which go to proof of the elements of the offence. So you can't say categorically across the board that if you can point to one fact that the Prosecutor has pleaded in the indictment that that then is the grounds upon which it should be dismissed. That, Your Honour, is a myth. Secondly, Your Honour, the question was raised yesterday about the exercise of prosecutorial discretion. It's a myth, Your Honour, that that's a defence. As Judge Jan correctly pointed out, was this matter raised with the Prosecutor. That's indeed what should happen if there's any questions about prosecutorial discretion. In this jurisdiction, indictments are drafted by the Prosecutor and submitted to a confirming Judge. If there's any question about the exercise of the discretion, that's a matter that needs to be taken up with the Prosecutor. It's not a matter that need trouble Your Honours, now, at all. To suggest that it is a matter that needs trouble Your Honours is a myth. There's been, in the course of these proceedings, a number of instances where we have had collateral attacks, if I can call it that, where instead of concentrating and focusing on the main point of the case, instead of challenging the Prosecution evidence and saying this is wrong and this is why my client is not guilty of this offence, because that evidence is incorrect, or whatever, we have had this series of collateral matters. The prosecutorial discretion issue that I mentioned is yet another one to be added to the top of attacks upon the Registrar, the interpreter, the guards, the accommodation, indeed, individual members of Your Honours' bench. So, why these issues are raised, Your Honours? They are raised in my respectful submission because attacking the Prosecution case directly exposes the weakness in the defence. And it's because they don't want you to see the weakness in their case that they raise all these peripheral collateral matters to otherwise consume Your Honours' time. The next matter, Your Honours, is in relation to Common Article 3 of the statute. Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions. It's been raised by Mr. Moran, I think he made it plain that he raised it because he wants to appeal it. He wants to persuade the Appeal Chamber to change its mind for all its previous decisions and say we got it wrong. Fair enough, if he needs to create a record for that, for those purposes, I can understand why he might want to do that. But so far as Your Honours' concern, you need not be concerned about that at all. It's a matter which has been decided by the Trial Chamber, by the Appeal Chambers, and Mr. Moran, I think, concedes that Your Honours are probably bound by it. There's two points, however, that I would like to address on this question, and it's not for the record. It's two points which have been made, I think, on numerous occasions, if not in this Chamber, before this Court, before the Appeals Chamber and in other cases. The first point is that if you're a successor state, then under the Treaty on Succession of States, Article 34, which at this stage has not come into force but is generally accepted as espousing the principles of international law, clearly states that a succeeding state carries with it and has, is obligated by international treaties which are binding upon the predecessor state. It's a simple concept but one that's generally accepted, Your Honours, and has been incorporated in this treaty. The effect of that is, Your Honours, that you need to look at the former Yugoslavia, and then the question is had it exceeded to the Geneva Conventions. Question is yes, no dispute about that, a long time ago, 1959, I think. Then is Bosnia bound by it in the early part of 1992? Yes, because of that principle. But also, in the exercise and application of that principle when the repository of states excision to treaties, the foreign ministry of the government of Switzerland, in relation to the Geneva Conventions, it accepts it from the date of independence, which in the case of Bosnia, is the 6th of March of 1992. So, any suggestion, Your Honours, that the Geneva Conventions had no application in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the relevant dates of our indictment is a myth. The question of whether Common Article 3 was intended by the security council to be incorporated and picked up and applied by Article 3 of our statute has been raised by the Defence in their submissions, as well. It's been suggested to Your Honours, it was never intended, that the security council had ever intended to incorporate Common Article 3 under Article 3 of our statute. The Defence raised the argument, look at the Rwanda statute, it's spelled out in the Rwanda statute. Obviously that was the position, it had to be expressly stated, otherwise it had no application, and it was never contemplated. Well, Your Honours only need to go to the debates of the security council on the adoption of the statute of the Tribunal of the Yugoslavia, for this Tribunal, the 25th of May 1993. It's the verbatim record of the 3.270th meeting of the Security Council, and read what the Ambassador for the United States, Madeline Albright, had to say about it at the time. And she says that she believes that it's the understanding of all of the members and that they share the view that Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions is incorporated and applied to the International Tribunal for Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Can you read the statement she made?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm reading from page 187 of the record of the minutes of the meeting. And this is Madeline Albright. "In particular, we understand that other members of the council share our view regarding the following clarifications related to the statute. Firstly, it's understood that the laws or customs of war referred to in Article 3," and she is referring to Article 3 of our statute, "include all obligations under humanitarian law agreements in force in the territory of the former Yugoslavia at the time the acts were committed, including Common Article 3 of the 1949 Geneva Conventions and the 1977 additional protocols of these conventions." Quite clear, Your Honours. The other issue that I might touch on now that we're talking about, Common Article 3, and it needs to be brief, is in relation to whom it applies to. And there seems to be some suggestion that there's doubt about that by these submissions that have been raised by the Defence. Your Honours, there's no doubt. It's very clear. Your Honours only have to read it. And as you have been encouraged to rely upon the plain words that appear in the statute, Your Honours only have to do that to see the ambit of its application. It applies to persons taking no active part in the hostilities, including members of the armed forces that have laid down their arms. Including. It is not limited only to those, Your Honours. So it has a very broad application, there's no question or doubt about that. The next myth, myth 4, if I can raise it quickly and dispose of it quickly; they is a suggestion that Your Honours may have seen in the submissions, written submissions of Mr. Delalic which speak of the prevailing conditions in Yugoslavia, in Bosnia in particular, Konjic area at the time. And the argument is mounted on the basis that if the government makes a good faith effort to provide conditions which would seek to comply with the Geneva Conventions, then that is sufficient. It's all it has to do. Myth, Your Honours. Myth for a number of reasons. Myth because it doesn't work that way. If you want to lock people up in the course of war, there's rules that says that they are conditions under which they must be kept. It's not good enough to say we tried but we didn't quite get they, things are pretty tough. No, that's not it. If you do it, the conventions are clear, you must comply with them. But really, was they a genuine attempt to ameliorate the conditions of these people kept in this camp? They was no question they was sufficient water. They is plenty of water they, the evidence shows that; just they wouldn't give it to them. They was no need to keep people in a tunnel. There's plenty of room. They didn't have to be kept in a tunnel. They was no need to beat them or torture them or kill them. They didn't have to do any of that. That's got nothing to do with conditions at the time. So, Your Honour, it's a myth. There's also another myth that's been raised in the written submissions of the Defence, Delalic, page 16. It's a somewhat convoluted argument and I'm not sure I fully follow it; but it is suggested to Your Honours that because the Celebici detainees don't set out, in detail, all the matters which go to describe a prisoner of war under the Geneva Conventions, that either they are liars or we are liars. Well, Your Honours, that's a fairly broad and sweeping generalisation, if it's intended to mean what it says, and I can only rely on the plain reading of their submission. We have never suggested at any stage, nor has any of the evidence of the Prosecution suggested that all of these people were prisoners of war under the Prisoners of War Convention. They were certainly detained. Some of them were civilians. And they are different categories of that convention, different categories in the Prisoners of War Convention which apply. They didn't come to Your Honours and precisely state what category they fell under, but a lot of them would have easily fallen under Category 46, in my submission, namely inhabitants of a non-occupied territory who on the approach of the enemy spontaneously take up arms to resist the invading forces, et cetera, Your Honours can read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Invading forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Invading forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You invade a foreign country, you don't invade your own country.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's an argument for the Defence. But it seems that the people -- they is a great deal of comment about who is doing what, and there's this curious argument which I will come to and, I think, answer in greater detail about this issue of whether it's an international armed conflict. Because the Defence speaks with forked tongues on this, and I will develop it shortly. But they say on one hand, well, they don't say, but they don't deny in a serious way that there's an international armed conflict going on. Not at all. Why could they do that? Well, because the very people they worked for, the very government that they worked for said it was an international armed conflict. So, they can't very well say, it doesn't sit well in their mouths to stand up now and say, Your Honour, this wasn't an armed conflict at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Whether it was an international conflict -- you have the resolution of the security council. It's an international conflict, maybe you have some point to make they. But invading force obviously means that some foreign force is invading a foreign territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we had here a situation of transition, the transition of secession, and the whole of this case has been argued by the defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I've not been able to make myself clear. Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised as a territory as an independent state. The forces going to Bradina, Konjic area, et cetera, were forces of Bosnian state. The Konjic area is part of Bosnia, so wouldn't these forces, the legal forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina be set to be invading a territory which has been internationally recognised as part of its own territory? That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the point, I'm using up a lot my valuable time, but I do want to persuade you on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I will give extra time to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The point of the matter is, Your Honours, that this is not a question of where everything was black and white. The fact of the matter is and it's an undeniable fact that they was a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina over which the forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at a point in time, had no control. It still exists to this day. It's called the Republic of Srpska, but the Republic of Srpska is an entity that shrunk from a larger entity, and the fact of the matter is that it shrunk because of a number of reasons, particularly in international intervention where lines were drawn, but it shrunk because of the fact it was taken over by the forces of army of the Bosnia-Herzegovina. Up until that time it was held by forces of a combination of the JNA, which represented the Serbian Bosnian Serbs, and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So, it was a part of the country, and these people were in that country and they knew that the advancing forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina was going to take over their territory. This is a period of transition. You can't just look at it and say this is black and that's white and that's the end of the matter. You've got to look at the facts. In my respectful submission, Your Honour, the fact of the matter is we were going through a process of change which is still happening to this day. Because of that, is the Geneva Conventions to be denied to these people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Before you go forward, don't you think you should limit this type of analogy to the particular facts of the case before us and where the prisoners were captured from, and whether those facts come within the purview of this argument? Because the prisoners were from Bradina and -- two places, these are the main areas where they were prisoners who were in Celebici camp, from those two areas, and these two areas come within that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And they do come within that context, Your Honour. They were territories which were occupied by people who were regarded as being hostile to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that's why, Your Honour, that the Geneva Conventions must apply to them in those circumstances. I may come back to just touch on some of those matters in a moment, Your Honour. One point, though, Your Honours, is when it comes to prisoners of war, the question of nationality doesn't arise, not mentioned. So if nationality is an issue, it's not in respect of people who would be prisoners of war. Myth 6, Your Honour. Question of whether diminished responsibility amounts to a Defence. Well, the first point we make, we made in our written submissions, we make it briefly again; in our submission their evidence just doesn't meet the defence. They haven't produced sufficient evidence to demonstrate that they was diminished responsibility. They haven't met their burden. That's clear from the evidence but I go on. There's a matter of law, Your Honours, diminished mental capacity is not a complete defence, and at most it would entitle an accused to a lesser sentence. So, it can't be sort of put up as a basis once we prove this, that's it, we're entitled to acquittal. The Defence have tried to incorporate English law, but the English law only applies to murder. So it has, if English law is to be applied, then Your Honours, it only has that limited application, it doesn't go to matters such as torture and the other crimes with which the accused Landzo has been charged. So, in our submission, Your Honours, firstly, diminished mental capacity hasn't been shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you very clear that the citation of the British law not be convicted of murder. That's all, but can be convicted of something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, can be a victim of manslaughter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I checked up on that. I'm trying to find out. It merely talks of murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I haven't got it with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It has a number of qualifications why he can't be convicted of murder. A number of qualifications they; but I was just wondering what happens then. Then he can be convicted of manslaughter?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I will see if I can find this out for you, Your Honour, but the alternative verdicts apply, murder manslaughter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Conceptually, if it is diminished responsibility, that is what the phrase means. Definitely it could be spread to any area of responsibility. I agree it is limited to murder, but definitely, conceptually it could be extended.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's not how it's understood in most jurisdictions with which I am familiar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, but you follow the context within which the concept itself originated because they were merely reducing homicide to manslaughter. Then if all it does is to diminish responsibility to committing an offence, if one can establish that, that responsibility is not the fullest, it should go accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As Your Honour is suggesting, it should go to all offences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I have not said so. I said if you can so show from the evidence which is available to the Tribunal, then one should be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It's a bit like the duress argument, Your Honours. There is nothing unusual, strange in having a law that says it applies, the defences only have limited application. The address argument is the other way around. It says duress is no defence to the killing of innocent human beings. That's been held by this Tribunal in the Erdemovic appeal case. But it has application to other offences, so it can apply to lesser offences. Which is the reverse of this argument, but it's the same concept and there is nothing unusual or strange about it. In this case -- you have in the United Kingdom and I don't profess to be an expert in the law of the United Kingdom -- but as I understand it in the United Kingdom, we have alternative verdicts, which is a very common provision in most states where you have murder, manslaughter, so the jury are given the option to return a verdict of murder or manslaughter under certain conditions. This is how this operates as I understand it. That if you establish diminished responsibility, you're entitled to the alternative verdict of manslaughter and that, of course, reduces the penalty which would otherwise apply. So, in our submissions, Your Honours, if the Defence are relying on English law and they take with it that concept as well, if they try and argue, well, we're entitled to raise the defence of diminished mental capacity. In so doing that, because there are no alternative verdicts recognised by this Tribunal, that means that we're entitled to jump the canal and get a full acquittal. That's not the way, in my respectful submission, it should be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, what our own evidence that allows us is to apply any law which is appropriate for the particular situation. So we're not bound to follow national laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It could be adjusted to fit the circumstances. In the interest of justice before us, we should be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I venture to suggest, Your Honours, that if you expanded the concept of diminished mental capacity to cover a situation where you're entitled to a complete acquittal, rather than a reduced sentence or an alternative verdict, then you'd be doing something which is quite novel to the common law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not saying we're doing that. But if the evidence is such that the nature of the diminished capacity is such that the person cannot even act, because none of the psychiatrists have given to us what the situation of the diminished capacity is, none of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think we've mentioned it in our submissions, Your Honours, at page 236 and following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I have read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Hopefully, Your Honours, in time, may have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: As far as that, as I read the English position, there has to be a finding that the accused is abnormal. It's only then that you give way to display. It has to be finding of fact that he is abnormal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next point, Your Honours, myth seven, if I can call it that, relates to the credibility of Prosecution witnesses. I have a number of points that I wish to make on this. Firstly, in the written submissions, there are numerous occasions where Your Honours are encouraged to look closely to the decision in the Tadic case and to rely on that for various points that would assist you in coming to your decision. Funnily enough, no mention is made of the issue of credibility of prosecution witnesses in Tadic case, in this respect. In the Tadic case, Your Honours -- and Your Honours, I may have to read the decision of Their Honours. In that case, you'll see that almost to a witness they were believed. And I am talking about the witnesses who are inmates in the Omarska, Trnopolje and Keraterm camps were accepted by the Courts as telling the truth. The Court may have made decisions about international armed conflict and all that other sorts of things, but when it came down to believing there witnesses, almost to a witness, they were believed. There witnesses, Your Honours, had the same sort of an axe to grind. Probably a bigger axe to grind and they came before the Court. They gave their story. They were inconsistent. They were nervous. There was interpreting problems. There was inconsistencies between statements. They were raised on a daily basis in there proceedings. The Defence made a big thing about this. And said, "How can you believe any of it"? One of the principle submissions they made is, how could you believe them, they have an axe to grind, they have every reason to come here and lie to you. That's not what the Tribunal found in that case. And these witnesses may also be accused of having an axe to grind. In my submission, Your Honours, they're equally believable as any of there witnesses in the Tadic case. The only distinction between the Tadic case and this case was that in the Tadic case, the majority of the witnesses were Muslim and in this case they were Serb. Your Honours, it's said that also that the Prosecution relies on the evidence of, I think at one stage it was said, we only rely on two witnesses, Mr. Landzo and Witness D, is a myth and I wish to correct that, Your Honours. It's interesting how the evidence of Mr. Landzo consistently corroborates many of the Prosecution witnesses. It's very interesting how he does that. And the Prosecution is entitled to point to that and say, "Look at this, Your Honours. Look at how he is saying something very, very similar and very close to what our witnesses said." We're entitled to do that, and we've done it and that's fair. But we're not only relying on Mr. Landzo for our case. And, Your Honours, when you come to read our submissions, I think you'll clearly see that that's the case. Then the Defence in this case have liked to raise this question that the Serb association has tampered with our witnesses and corrupted them and there is talk of this seminar, which is a mystery to me, which has been had so they can only be tutored and come before you and give this tutored, structured evidence. It's very interesting that I'd make that argument and at the same time talk to inconsistencies and say there is inconsistencies and yet they've been tutored. It would be a fairly poor job of tutoring, if that was the case. Your Honours, when this question was raised with the witnesses, every witness refuted that they had been lectured, they had been tutored in giving evidence. The so-called meeting of the witnesses in Romania, which is sort of described as a seminar, if you please, it happened to be a meeting with the investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor who met with the witnesses in Romania because they were precluded and prevented from going on to the territory of the former Yugoslavia in order to gather the evidence of this case. Another myth that has been raised is the question of the calling of the witness, Ramic. It's been said that we didn't call him because his evidence would have been exculpatory. So, therefore, Your Honours were deprived of hearing his evidence. Your Honours that's an extraordinary thing to say. There are many, many reasons why witnesses are called and not called and there is no reason why the Defence couldn't have called this witness. So if he had something exculpatory to say, do you think that they would have been up there in the first witness. Come along, Mr. Ramic, and tell the Chamber about this exculpatory evidence. Not a bit of it. We didn't hear anything from them in that regard. So it's a sweeping, broad generalisation, Your Honours. It's a myth. It's said about the witness, Assad Harraz. He is a credible witness and whatever you believe, fine. We accept that. What we also ask Your Honours to accept is his evidence about Mr. Delalic being the overall commander of the area. We ask you to accept that he spoke of Mr. Mucic as being commander of the camp and his article in Exhibit 167 is the 24th of July, 1992, so that's before the 27th of July, 1992. Your Honours, you may have been there and didn't see things that happened on another day, that doesn't make him a liar. That doesn't make the Prosecution witnesses a liar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is one thing about the Prosecution witnesses. It is said, many of them said they were beaten up in front of this crew which is led by this particular witness for the Prosecution. This position was now clarified by you when he appeared in the witness box.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I agree that there is some issue there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That does affect credibility of the witnesses who make such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It might affect the credibility of Mr. Harraz. But, Your Honours, the point I wish to make on that, is that there has never been any actual certainty that he was the only Arab journalist that visited the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think there is some evidence. It is the only thing he visited. I think there is some evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, my understanding -- Your Honours, no doubt have a better understanding of the evidence than me. But my understanding was -- it's always open. It's a big stretch, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am just thinking, maybe the witnesses of the Prosecution have made such exaggerations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's always possible, Your Honours. At the end of the day only you can decide that question. It's entirely possible that either Mr. Harraz may have made an exaggeration or may not have told something which happened, or it may have been the case for the prosecution witness. But it doesn't mean, Your Honours, they're liars. It doesn't mean they're liars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Exaggeration is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It's not a lie. So, one doesn't immediately dismiss a witness out of hand simply because they portray something differently than somebody else portrays it. I don't know Mr. Harraz's background at all, frankly. Things that he may not consider to be serious, others may, I don't know. Going on to the other witness that was challenged, Risto Vukalo. Your Honours, because I am running short of time, I do encourage you to go to the evidence and read this. I think you'll agree with me when you go to the evidence that it's very clear that what's happened there when Mr. Moran is discussing this question which he relies upon to demonstrate what he says is the fact that this witness can't be relied on, is a confusion. It's a clear confusion. Mr. Moran says -- and I will quote shortly what he says in the transcript. He says, "It would be in early January 1993," and he is talking about a beating in the Musala camp. "Right before you made that statement to there investigators from a Bosnian army, a couple of days before, that is what you said, is it not?" So he specifically raises the statement given to officers of the Bosnian army. Specifically does that. And about 20 lines later, he says show the witness the statement by the Office of the Prosecutor and says, "Read it." The witness reads it. And Mr. Moran says -- reads that out and then the witness says this and this is the point that I wish to make. "Sir, I had it stated that way. If they had told me that milk was black" -- they, in my respectful submission, is clearly the Bosnian army investigators. "I would have had to say that, lest I be treated the same way I was treated in Celebici. Lest in Musala I was treated the same way as I was treated in Celebici. I was afraid of that. Who dared to say that there were beatings going on in Musala." Clearly the witness is confused and one can understand why the witness is confused. He mentioned a statement he gave to the Bosnian investigators in 1993 and then you hand him an OTP statement. Again, the situation with respect to Witness T and Grozdana Cecez. Your Honours, the issue on that is identification. The transcript page is page 6.782. Your Honour, Judge Karibi-Whyte, picked that up immediately and said it was the person who raped her that she didn't know about at that time. That's not the rape that's in the charge. That's the Witness T, alleged Witness T rape. And so there was confusion over that issue. No confusion whether she knew him from some other occasion. Now, Your Honours there are numerous cases that, Your Honours are as well aware of as I am, that fall into that category where rapes have occurred, even by people that the victims know about and they didn't -- they weren't able to identify in the circumstances. Your Honours, finally, we come to the last myth that I would seek to destroy, if I may. It relates to the question of international armed conflict. I have touched upon a number of these matters so far and so I won't labour the issue by repeating them again. But, I have mentioned the fact of the attitude of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbinisation of the JNA, that is, that an army which was the federal army for the whole of the former Yugoslavia was converted into an army of the Republic of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It no longer was an army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at all. That's denied in the argument from the Defence. They never say anything about the bombardment of Konjic by the air force of the JNA. Are they suggesting to you that when Konjic was bombed that that was some sort of internal conflict? Is that the submission? No, Your Honour, they're not saying that. They're not saying anything. They're not saying that. I put it to you that the Serbinised JNA, when it bombed Konjic, was an international armed conflict and it was right in the town of Konjic. There is no question about that, Your Honours. Your Honour, Mr. Greaves, when he spoke to you, spoke about this question about what do you rely on when you come to looking at the offences charged in the statute? Do you look at the statute of the Tribunal, the ICTY statute? Or, do you look at the Geneva Conventions, themselves, directly? And which ones do you rely on primarily in assisting you in interpreting the law to be applied? Mr. Moran will tell you, no question, look at the Geneva Conventions, the tribunals of the security counsel can't make laws, so therefore the only relevant law is the Geneva Conventions. Mr. Greaves would urge you the other way. In my respectful submission, I believe that Mr. Greaves' argument stands up to better scrutiny. Of course, the security counsel didn't create new offences. It merely picked up and implied offences that are already there. There is no question about that. It did it in the statute of the Tribunal. But, Your Honours, when you're looking at this question, it's necessary to look at both documents, the statute of the Tribunal and the Geneva Conventions and to understand, as Your Honours no doubt do, but to understand consciously what the Geneva Conventions are doing. And what they're doing is they're trying to -- well, not trying to, they do in fact -- embrace two concepts. One concept is the concept of state enforcement of international law. So that's for state courts to apply international law. The other concept is the concept of International Tribunals enforcing international law under the Geneva Conventions. Now, Your Honours, unlike International Tribunals such as yourselves, state courts are much more concerned with the issue of extraterritorial jurisdiction. Why? Because state courts are careful not to offend foreign courts by usurping authority over what's happened in their foreign country and exercising jurisdiction. So state courts hold back, unless they're given specific legislation to say, you should go ahead and do this -- and this has happened in numerous countries, including Britain, which prosecutes offences that occurred during the Second World War in Europe, war crimes and so forth. As it expressly does say, the courts are very slow to exercise extra jurisdiction. This was no doubt in the minds of the drafters of the Geneva Conventions when they created the conventions, and no doubt the concept of international jurisdiction came about as a result of that. But one of the things that was inserted in there for the assistance of state courts -- and I promise I'll be very quick, Your Honours -- one of the things that was inserted in there was Article 2, which related to the issue of international armed conflict. So that before a state court made that jump and stepped in and exercised jurisdiction, in a matter in another country, it looked to the question of whether or not there was an international armed conflict. That's not, in my respectful submission, a matter that needs concern Your Honours. Your Honours need not be so concerned with exercising jurisdiction in another country. You are the product of the community of nations. Therefore the issue of being concerned about breaches of sovereignty are not a matter that need trouble you. In your own statute, the statute of the Tribunal, in Articles 6 and Articles 8, you are specifically given jurisdiction, territorial jurisdiction. Now, against that background, if you look at Article 2 of the Statute, which applies the grave breach provisions, there is no reference to international armed conflict at all. I raise this submission for Your Honours' consideration. In my submission, it's not a matter that need concern you. It's not a matter that's an element of the offence. It's a matter that may be an issue that could be raised by the Defence as to argue why the conventions don't apply or the grave breach provisions don't apply. It's not a matter that must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. And I say that, and it might be a surprising that I say this now at this stage of the proceedings. There is no question that the evidence of the Prosecutor proves beyond a reasonable doubt that this was an international armed conflict. The point I make is that you don't have to do it. It's not mentioned in Article 2 of the Statute. You're not concerned with issues of sovereignty, you're not concerned with issues of the community of nations, so it's not a matter that need concern Your Honours. You're clearly given your jurisdiction under Articles 6 and Articles 8 and that's where you can look to see whether you can determine this case before the Court. These matters are too serious. These events too tragic to have them dismissed from court on the grounds of a technicality, a technicality that should not concern Your Honours. Unless I can assist Your Honours with any other matters, there are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you have any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, a few things. Technicality. Technicality. What in the world is a technicality? We're not dealing with technicalities, we're dealing with the law. We're dealing with what the law defines as violations. If it's not defined as a violation, it's not a technicality to say the law doesn't apply. I can't believe what I just heard. Judge, in some ways, in the last hour or so, somebody has been trying to throw a little sand in your eyes and let me see if I can get a little of it out. Somebody has been trying to blur your vision, Judge. Let's start --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You want to get him out? You want to ensure it is out of the eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: We'll try to, at least, clear your vision a little bit, Judge. First thing is, the last time I checked from April 6th, 1992, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a nation just like Australia, just like the United States of America, just like the United Kingdom and it had defined boundaries, just like Australia, just like the United States of America and just like the United Kingdom. How a person can sit up here and say the Republic of Srpska, whatever they were doing, this, that and the other thing, how in the world does the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina invade the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? I am sure Mr. Niemann would be happy to tell you that on June 6th, 1944, when the Gaullist troops landed with the allies in Normandy, the French were invading France and the Germans were happily defending this country. You have to look at the Dayton Accords. My Secretary of State was in Sarajevo just yesterday talking about the Dayton Accords and how it's one country, always been one country, since April the 6th, 1992. He is trying to make -- he is got a set of facts and he's trying to define a crime to fit those facts and it just doesn't fit. There seems to be some problem with the difference between state succession and state secession. The Prosecutor has taken the position at various times in this trial, through his witnesses and in his written submissions, that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, according to Dr. Economides, led by Mr. Niemann ended in September 1992. Professor Gow says the latest was April 27th. In their written submission here they seem to accept April 27th, '92. That wasn't a matter of state succession, that one state succeeded another on April 6th,'92 when Bosnia-Herzegovina -- that was state secession. State succession is when Zaire became the democratic Republic of the Congo. A different government replaced an existing government. Read Professor Bassiouni book. He says that -- By the way, as far as I know, the United Nations has never recognised any state as being a successor state. To this great, good day, the federal Republic of Yugoslavia claims to be a successor state and has not been accepted as that by the General Assembly and the Security Council. I believe I have given the Trial Chamber several resolutions from the Security Council on exactly that matter. He takes the position when the Swiss foreign ministry accepts the articles of ratification from the Bosnian government in December 1992, it reflects back to April the 6th, '92. For purposes of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I have no problem with that. But he is also saying that if an offence occurred on -- pick a date, July 1st, 1992, at a time when the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina was not party to the conventions, that because of an act of that government, later, a criminal statute applies to individuals. Seems like a problem to me. Am I bound by the policies of Bosnia-Herzegovina? I don't think so. Is my client bound -- because the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina takes a position on an issue of law, does that mean that this Trial Chamber is bound? Does that mean then that if they drag in a citizen of the federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Trial Chamber 3 or Trial Chamber 1 would be bound by the policies of the federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I'll bet Mr. Niemann wouldn't like that. I'll bet he wouldn't like that a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Moran I have just a question. There is a creation of a statute passed by the security counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Can you say, or that the statute states, take jurisdiction in these matters, contraventions of the Geneva Conventions and can you say, no we can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You mean in contravention of the convention, Your Honour? In something different than in the convention?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We're saying conventions are not applicable because the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina had not -- can you say, no, we don't have jurisdiction. We're a creation of that statute, how can we challenge the legality of that statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand your question now. A couple of things. First, the statute and let's pick an article that doesn't apply to us, the genocide provision of our statute. It gives the Court jurisdiction to decide if there were violations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Let's look at the provisions of the Statute. You should have the jurisdiction. Can you say, we don't have the jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, you have the jurisdiction, no question about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That had the power to prosecute, persons responsible for serious violations of Article 1. It's followed by similar language in Article 2. Can you say, no, you don't have the jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. You clearly have the jurisdiction. The question before you is not whether the jurisdiction of the Tribunal because it's more than just this Trial Chamber -- has the jurisdiction to prosecute persons committing or ordering to be committed grave breaches. Clearly you do. The question I am presenting is, if Bosnia-Herzegovina was not at party, at the times applicable to this, could anyone who was acting an as agent of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina commit a grave breach if that did not apply to them? That is the issue that I am presenting. Clearly after December 31, Bosnia-Herzegovina became a party to the conventions and so I am presenting a slightly different, in fact, substantially different argument. Credibility of witnesses. In the Tadic case three Judges of this Court sat in the same three chairs you're sitting in and looked at the witnesses and judged credibility. I don't think the fact that they thought witnesses were credible in the Tadic case really is very binding on you in whether witnesses are credible in this case. I think that's an absurd argument. I do think we ought to point out, and one of my colleagues asked me to point it out, that in all innocence, the Office of the Prosecutor called a witness who was a card-carrying perjurer and presented him as a witness of the truth. Judge Jan, you hit the nail right on the head on one thing about Mr. Harraz. He gets up and says he is a credible guy, believe him about this and believe him about that; but how about believing when he denies filming or taking part in beatings of inmates in Celebici? Judge Jan, on at least two occasions I recall, one of which I can find in the transcript because I'm not as good at computers as I thought I was, you asked witnesses for the Office of the Prosecutor how many times there were Arab journalists. And every time I recall you asking that question the response was one. Risto Vukalo, look at the videotapes. After that experience, even Mr. Niemann was laughing, as I recall. Another thing that was just tossed out at you was the bombing of Konjic by the JNA air force. I have been informed by one of my colleagues that it is in the record that that occurred on May 10th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I thought this was the Ljuta barracks, where they were taking out certain ammunition that was stocked there, that this place was bombarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I recall a videotape shot in Konjic with actually the aircraft --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Much of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As I recall the air attacks were on the city, on Konjic. And as I recall, one of my colleagues, Mrs. Residovic pointed it out to me, that that occurred on the 10th of May, 1992. We have suggested that the Trial Chamber accept the formulation on international internal armed conflict that was used by Commander Fenrick, a member of the commission on experts, when he reported to the Canadian government, his government, that before April 6th it was an internal armed conflict, April 6th to May 19th, the order splitting the JNA, international.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But there is another aspect, whether it is international conflict or not. I think the best evidence would be provided by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Their own declaration of war naming the parties who committed the aggression, would that not be evidence of it being an international armed conflict? Because the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina is a proper body to say whether it is internal conflict or international armed conflict. Apart from that, you have all of the government of Serbia said that we were drawing up forces from there. But then there is a resolution of the security council imposing comprehensive sanctions on Serbia saying that they had not complied with the earlier direction of withdrawal. So, at least on the 30th of May when the security council imposes comprehensive sanctions against the government, the security council (inaudible).

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let me answer it a couple of ways, and if I don't answer it satisfactorily keep coming with questions and I'll work until I can. The first thing I would say is while the position of Bosnia-Herzegovina may be some evidence, I think it is clearly not binding upon the Trial Chamber. If you want to look at evidence, you can look in the Prosecutor's own written submission to you on the May 22nd agreement signed by Izetbegovic and the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It was to be ratified, and I think I did raise this question when the trial was going on whether someone ratified it or not; and I think the answer was no. Only if a certain thing happened, and that thing did not happen, how can you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was an agreement under Common Article 3, and the parties to that agreement, which the Prosecutor tells you the parties of the conflict, in their written submission, were the SDA, the SDS, the Bosnian Croatian community and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Supervised by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And the Red Cross, also, no question about that, Your Honour. In fact, this kind of Article 3 agreement, the Red Cross is only going to try and get if the Red Cross believes it is an internal armed conflict. So, if internal armed conflict breaks out in, pick a country, the Philippines, the Red Cross is going to try and get one of those. As for the United Nations and the security council's resolutions, Your Honour, I would suggest to you that if those are binding upon this Trial Chamber and upon the Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: A piece of evidence of which you can take judicial notice, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Again, it's like the position of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it is some evidence. You can take it for what it is worth. You're not bound by it. You may be a creature, you being the Tribunal, may be a creature of the security council, but you are not bound in your judicial duties by that. That would be a horrible depravation of every right in the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is a piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Where do you get your evidence about internationality of armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Internationality of armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Where do you get your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, you do it the same way the Tadic Trial Chamber did. You look at the evidence presented to you. You look at May 19th order. You look at the other factors that are there and you make that kind of reasoned judgement. You decide whether they have proven beyond a reasonable doubt. They pled it, they have to prove it. Especially in the Article 2 counts. I mean, that's clear. They have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that there was an international armed conflict or we don't get any further than that. You look at the Prosecutor's proof. I believe it comes under the presumption of innocence in Article 21 of the statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's a different answer than what I asked. I said, where do you get evidence of armed conflicts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Of armed conflict and the nature of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There are a lot of places, Your Honour. You get evidence from the witness stand. You have, they brought in two experts, Gow and Calic. You get evidence from them. You weigh the credibility of that evidence. You look at other testimony. You look at the testimony of Witness R. Excuse me, not Witness R, Witness M. Just because it happens to be sitting in front of me, residents that were brought in received no orders from the Republic of Srpska army. Is the republic -- the biggest thing I think you have to look at, and it is an evidentiary problem and something they have to prove, is the relationship between the army of the Republic of Srpska, the rebels, if you would, and the relationship with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That's, frankly, the issue that the Tadic Trial Chamber had a problem with. It's an evidentiary problem. You look at who controlled what. And if, you look to see if they brought you evidence that convinces you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I just asked you this so you will not simplify it as much as you have been doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I have oversimplified, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's so I know what I'm finding when I'm looking at evidence before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let me see, let me flip through my notes real quickly and see if I can give you some time back. The Prosecutor's position that it doesn't make any difference for the grave breaches provisions of the conventions, whether or not it was an internal or international armed conflict, first, has no foundation in law. It has no foundation in fact and it's contrary to the Tadic Appeals Chamber decision. That's just an incredible thing for them to say. It just takes a plain reading of the statute. Exaggeration is not a lie. Take that for what it's worth. Levee en masse, we talked about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Touch only those areas where you find --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm just flipping through my notes to make sure I cover everything I wanted to cover. Application of Common Article 3 and whether it's incorporated into Article 3 of the statute. The Secretary-General knew what he was doing when he wrote the report that accompanied the statute of this Tribunal to the security council. Presumably he knew what he was doing when he wrote the report that accompanied the statute of the Rwanda Tribunal to the same security council. That is the best evidence of the legislative intent, because the security council adopted his report along with the two statutes. I think that's awfully good proof. I've cited several other sources, Professor Bassiouni and others on whether or not Common Article 3 comes within your Article 3 jurisdiction. You're right, I am going to appeal it, or at least I'm presenting the issue to you because I think I have to. You may very well be bound by the Tadic Appeals Chamber decision. I'm not going to argue with Mr. Niemann over that. I hadn't said anything about this, either, yesterday, or I wasn't really planning on saying anything about this today, but I noticed in my notes there was that thing about witness school, the witness seminars, the allegations on that. I don't know whether there was or whether there wasn't. I wasn't invited, if there was one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You're not a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's true. But let me suggest this to you in judging the credibility of the witnesses. From the beginning of the trial somebody would get -- there would be some discussion about your prior statement, or you did this or that, or on cross, and you would get an "I don't recall," and you got "I don't remember, I don't remember, I don't remember, I don't remember, I don't remember, I don't remember," witness after witness after witness. And then all of a sudden people didn't have a problem not remembering, they had interpretation problems. And then there was a whole series of interpretation problems. And then the interpretation problems stopped and these prior statements were coerced out of them. And it ran in a series. Now, I'm a believer that there is such a thing as coincidence, but sometimes it goes a little far. So, I think the Trial Chamber can look at that in judging the credibility of witnesses. The credibility of Esad Landzo, you're going to have to judge what it is. You're talking about the guy who is the last witness in the trial, he has heard every bit of evidence and he has a computer with the transcripts on it, you know that because he told you that. You got a guy whose own psychiatrist says he is a sociopath. If you want to believe him, fine. I can't stop you. You're welcome to do it. Unless the Court has some other questions, I'm going to thank you for your time this morning and if I took -- actually it was 21 minutes, I think I did pretty well, given my record of running overtime, and I thank you very much, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any other contribution?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, yesterday I took five minutes more of your time. I promise that I won't use my 20 minutes today for my right to reply. I should also like to apologise, I have a slight cold, so, I am not going to articulate as well as possible. I would like to speak about two matters which the Prosecutor brought up in his closing arguments today. The question of myth. The Prosecutor tells us that we are talking about a myth by saying that each and every fact, small fact has to be proved; whereas, they say that you prove the case as a whole, and in that sense they have the evidence on their side. Second, they maintain that the Defence wishes to attack the discretion of the Prosecutor, and in that way, once again, to speak about a myth. The Defence does not wish to bring up any myths. We wish to speak about the facts before this Tribunal and the basic laws and rules underlining every criminal case; and that is that the Prosecutor must place the facts before this Court to be proved beyond any reasonable doubt. And the Defence of Mr. Delalic maintains that the Prosecutor has not spoken about any fact which has to do with Delalic’s authority has proved beyond reasonable doubt, that they have not proved any of these facts. We do not base our assumptions on myths, but we base them on facts and proof and evidence provided by the Prosecutor and by the Defence alike. None of the witnesses, neither the Prosecution witness or the Defence witnesses confirmed or stated a single word which could determine that Zejnil Delalic was a person in superior authority in the sense of Article 7.3 of the statute, nor that he committed any acts for which he is personally responsible in the sense of Article 7.1 of the statute. I will remind you of two witnesses, the late General Pasalic and General Divjak, both Prosecution witnesses. In connection with the facts, what facts state, and not myths, let me also remind you that the Prosecutor very often, before us and before you, Your Honours, said that he wanted to have the truth determined before this Tribunal. And I'm going to say that it is true that the Prosecutor has a discretionary right as to who he is going to bring before the Tribunal, just as the Defence enjoys the same right. But, the Prosecutor himself, in his investigations, listened to the witnesses which you heard here, that is to say Dr. Rusmir Hadzihuseinovic, DC-4, Bajram Demic, Redzepovic Enver, the first commander of the TO of Konjic, Polutak Mustafa, the first commander of tactical group one. None of those were brought by the Prosecutor to the Tribunal, to the Chamber. They were brought by the Defence itself. That is the truth, Your Honours, which we should like to indicate and for which we say that the evidence presented before this Trial Chamber are not myth, but facts which confirm that the Prosecutor, vis-à-vis Zejnil Delalic, has not succeeded in proving a single one of those facts. He has not succeeded in proving beyond all reasonable doubt that, at any time, Zejnil Delalic had a position of superiority. I should also like to tell you, Your Honours, and that is something that the Prosecution is well aware of, that Zejnil Delalic already in May 1996 quite openly suggested an exchange of evidence, and up to July 1996 supplied the Prosecutor with all the statements of the individuals who were investigated and they all said the same thing, that Zejnil Delalic gave the Prosecution evidence, that is he gave orders dating the 24th of August and the 28th of August because he had nothing to hide. He transferred the orders of the Supreme Command to the municipal staff. And you heard General Polutak, not this conveyance of orders, but a combat order to a combat unit. This was transferred by Polutak as commander of the tactical group and ordered that it pass through occupied territory of Gorazde. So the assertion of the Prosecutor that the conveyance complies with the chain of command, this has not been borne out by the evidence. When we are talking about the myth that is being offered, I did not want to raise this matter yesterday, but I should just like to remind you today of two points from the written submission of the Prosecutor. When there are no facts, then the Prosecutor offers something that is not a fact. What does he do? Namely, in point 430 C, page 166, the Prosecutor tells us that his witness, just imagine that, General Divjak, who visited, together with Mr. Delalic, the warehouses, ammunition warehouses that you see over there; he does not say that, he says when they visited Celebici that he considered that Celebici were under the command and control of Mr. Delalic. On the page that the Prosecutor quotes, General Divjak says, "I, with Mr. Delalic visited the ammunitions warehouse," and when asked by the Prosecutor under whose authority were they, he says that the ammunition warehouses I think were under the competency and authority of the TG2 group, Mr. Delalic. And when you, Your Honours, asked on page 8.683 under whose authority was the prison? General Divjak answers and says, "I think it was under the authority of the municipal staff." Therefore, it is the facts that you are going to appraise, and it is the facts that stand up in defence of Mr. Delalic and not myths. For this reason yesterday we quoted the example of the failure to call one of the commanders, Esad Ramic, because he was brought under subpoena by the Prosecutor, because he convinced the Trial Chamber that the subpoena was necessary, because he had something to say; whereas, the witness did not enter this courtroom. In that way, that is how facts are viewed, and we do not make myths out of facts, we have facts. I know, Your Honours, that you are also going to take all the other facts into consideration. In the written submissions there are some other assertions stated to be in the evidence which is not there. Let me quote two. It is maintained in point 4155 that Zejnil Delalic 8 appointed Pavo Mucic in written form. If you take a look at this, Pavo Mucic never said that. Although, there is your decision that the statement of one individual cannot be used against another defendant. The next question I wish to raise is something that we heard comment about by my colleague, and that is that it was unthinkable for me to hear the explanations by the Prosecutor as to whether Bosnia-Herzegovina is a state and whether it has the right to control its own territory or not. That is on the 6th of April recognised and on the 22nd of May accepted into the United Nations; and let me remind you of the words of General Divjak, the Prosecution's witness, who in that independent state took Ivan Sedlo, the Thermopile of Bosnia, on its own territory. It is the question of that territory's defence and every commander who would not try to deblock a town like Konjic, then the commander would be the responsible commander. Unfortunately, in Sarajevo, for four years, we tried to liberate ourselves, but we were not able to do this without the help of the international community. And the last thing that I want to say is the following. It was stated that the Defence has no feeling for the victims. I did not want to raise this question yesterday because this Trial Chamber and its statute relies on individual responsibility; but these are the first individuals who have been brought before an international court of law who were, at the same time, the victims. They were in the country and the town that was under attack. And the Prosecutor has not yet brought forward somebody from another state which was also attacked, as a reaction, and then committed a crime in that sense; because the provisions and rules of this Tribunal allow for that. We cannot be accused of not having feelings, whether somebody was murdered, whether he was mistreated, left to go hungry. Perhaps the Prosecutor will call upon me as a victim of a town where 12.500 people were killed and 5500 were wounded, perhaps I will be called to 25 testify, or my 13 year old child who tried to help me get up as I lay wounded. So, we do have feelings for victims, because we were all victims, we were all killed, we all had to go hungry, we were all wounded and injured and had to live in the dark. But we're not discussing feelings in this Trial Chamber. We are discussing whether the Prosecutor has been able to show beyond any reasonable doubt the facts as they stand. And Your Honours, I know that with those facts before you, you will ascertain that the Prosecutor has not proved beyond reasonable doubt, not one single fact with regard to Zejnil Delalic Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you, we will now have a break and reassemble at 12.00

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, may we hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I know one of the biggest myths that lawyers say is, we'll be brief. But I will be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In these circumstances you are expected to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to talk on just a couple of issues. The first issue is the international armed conflict issue. I would like to cite the Court to pages 278 and 279 of the Prosecution's submission on the issue of whom they consider to be parties to the conflict. That being Serbian Democratic Party, the Croatian Democratic Community and the Party of Democratic Action. I think that amounts to an admission of who they think the parties of the conflict are. Further on that issue, I would like to point the Court to something that's somewhat simplistic, but I think it's very apropos. Pull out a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina and take a look of where Konjic lies. If this was an issue involving perhaps Belijna and Zvornik, which is right on the border of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Perhaps there may be a more compelling argument to the issue of international armed conflict, but given where this occurred -- and General Divjak in his testimony talked about this and we talk about it in our submission -- it's more of a local conflict in this area between local people. The other issue I wanted to talk about just briefly is a comment by the Prosecutor in his rebuttal about the governments for which the defence works or the government for which the defence works, wanting this to be an international armed conflict. I am not supposing that that means that the lawyers and their clients are employees of the government, I think that's just the position that the prosecution is taking the government has itself and not the attorneys. But I wanted to point that out. I am glad to hear that Mr. Mucic's lack of authority in Celebici is not considered to be a myth by the Prosecution in its rebuttal. I think two important things we'd like you to look at with respect to Mr. Mucic and command responsibility, command authority: One is, Mr. Delalic is alleged to have appointed Mr. Mucic. And if Mr. Delalic has not appointed Mucic, then the question must be asked, well where did that come from? Where did that authority flow from? Because the indictment flows from the top to the bottom with respect to command responsibility. And if Mr. Delalic didn't appointment Mr. Mucic, then who did? There is no evidence one way or the other. In a society, I think this is true in most regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia and wherever, which is fixated on stamps and signatures and documents, you see before you this cart of hundreds and hundreds of documents and not one of those documents indicates any appointment of Mr. Mucic, any parameters for Mr. Mucic with respect to Celebici out of the hundreds and hundreds of documents that sit before you. Finally, I would like to point out that on the issue of whether or not the indictment needs to be proven beyond a reasonable doubt, meaning the facts, I do believe that the Prosecution has a burden to prove up the facts in the indictment. Obviously you don't have to prove up every single fact within the whole case. But the indictment in and of itself is the indictment upon which the accused must stand trial. And the Prosecution has that burden to prove the allegations within the entire indictment, not just part of the indictment, beyond a reasonable doubt. And, for these reasons, we believe Mr. Mucic should be acquitted. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you, very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: May it please the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Landzo was never called a sociopath by anyone in the testimony before this Court. Dr. Gripon used anti-social. Sociopath was a creation made by Mr. Delic's attorney. Mr. Delic's total defence has been that everybody that testified from that witness stand was incredible, was lying. As I promised Judge Jan, I am now going to read into the record, the submission of the Defence on what the definition of torture should be from the Defence perspective. And under the Geneva Convention and under -- we wish to accept to propose the definition of torture used by the ICRC in which it says that torture is more than mere assault on the physical and moral integrity and torture is the infliction of suffering on a person to obtain from that person or from another person, confessions or information. What is important is not so much the pain itself as the purpose of its infliction. It's much narrower than the Prosecution submission on torture, which, of course, includes such vague considerations as to intimidate or coerce. So we believe that this submission should be limited for the purposes described in the Geneva Convention as applies to warfare. Now, Mr. Niemann also talked to us about prosecutorial discretion. I preferred to call it selective Prosecution yesterday, but Mr. Niemann has called it prosecutorial discretion. Mr. Niemann and Judge Jan asked if I had taken up that subject with the Prosecutor herself. I have to admit that I was remiss that I had not taken that up with the Prosecutor. But this morning we hand delivered a letter to Ms. Arbour to please consider under Article 21 and under the guarantees of equity in this Tribunal that the indictment against Mr. Landzo be dismissed. And Mr. Niemann claims that Tribunal Chamber does not have the right to interfere with prosecutorial discretion. The truth is that this Trial Chamber is here to guarantee and protect the guarantees under the statute of this tribunal. And one of the guarantees is equality. And as Judge Karibi-Whyte says, that he stated on many occasion, that this Trial Chamber has the duty to see that justice is served. Also, as Mr. Kuzmanovic had stated, Mr. Niemann is seeking to limit the proof of the Prosecutor to merely the elements of the offence as he described it. Well, when you read our statute, there are no specific elements outlined. But in almost all jurisdictions outside of this Tribunal and probably adopted by this Tribunal, they hold the Prosecutor to proving every allegation asserted in the indictment. So to say that the burden is something less flies in the face of the rights of the accused guaranteed under Article 21. Not only is he tempted the limit the burden, he is almost shifting the burden by saying that he does not have to prove every allegation in the indictment. There have been several attempts of Esad Landzo to come before this Trial Chamber and tell the truth over the past two years. The first time in 1996 he asked his Bosnian lawyer to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to apologise to the interpreters right now. I do tend to talk fast. I will be giving back time, so I can slow down this time. But he tried to cooperate at that point. He reached out to Ms. McHenry at the end of 1996, saying that in a letter that he wanted to be executed by a firing squad and wanted to discuss things with her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In fact, I had a meeting with Ms. McHenry and Mr. Niemann in the summer of 1997 saying that he wanted to cooperate. But his lead counsel did not consent to that then, so our proposals were not considered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Proposal for execution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, I didn't reach out to them to have him executed, I reached out to them to see if we could see if we could reach some kind of agreement for cooperation. He also sought to tell truth by asking his witnesses who had previously agreed to come before this Trial Chamber and testify who subsequently, right before testifying, were somehow persuaded not to come by other sources to come and tell the truth and they refused. At the risk of his life and the life of his family, he has come here to tell the truth. This decision, this risk, should not be taken so lightly. Mr. Niemann keeps describing these myths. His sixth myth that he alleged that diminished mental responsibility is not a Defence. That's exactly the statement he said in opening that section up. The Homicide Act of 1957 labelled it a defence as a matter of law. The Rome statute, which was adopted in July, but for the rules promulgated for in a permanent international court to be established says that diminished mental responsibility is a law. And the laws of this Tribunal clearly say that as a matter of law, diminished responsibility is a Defence. It's not merely mitigation of punishment. Judge Karibi-Whyte correctly recognised that this Trial Chamber can apply any law it feels is appropriate in the interest of justice. We're not bound by national laws or state laws. Now, we had to prove beyond a preponderance of the evidence that Esad Landzo suffered from an abnormality of mind that substantially impaired his ability to exercise his free will and decisions in the Celebici camp in 1992. We had to prove that by a preponderance of the probabilities, the lowest burden of proof in any legal system. We have met that burden of proof with this Trial Chamber, with the evidence put forth. Now, Mr. Niemann also talked about myth seven, was that the Prosecution witnesses were incredible or uncredible. And Mr. Niemann should be most familiar as all as mentioned before with the hidden political agendas of persons coming before this Tribunal to testify. In fact, he knows that once in his zeal as an advocate, maybe he didn't ask the right question to ask if his witness was telling the truth. And maybe that witness was subsequently charged with perjury before this Trial Chamber. He talked about the association of detainees. He said he never heard of the witnesses going up there and talking about their stories with each other. He never heard that the association of detainees interfered here. Well, it's my submission that Mr. Niemann was not present during most of the Prosecutor's case. And if he'd only look at one in particular, Mici Kuljanin, who testified for the Prosecution, on cross-examination by one Defence counsel, he said, no, he had never met with the association of detainees and he did not have an escort. That very evening he was found in the presence of the representative of the association of detainees and another testifying witness down at the beach. And that was brought out on cross-examination the following day. Mr. Niemann just needs to review the evidence in this case to be aware of the interference of the association of detainees from Belgrade. Now, Mr. Niemann may claim that all the evidence in this case put forth by the Defence is a myth. And Ms. McHenry may claim that the Defence of diminished mental responsibility is a joke, but this approach by the Prosecution, a body set out to search for justice and truth, is a conundrum, an oxymoron. This past 18 months has been taken very seriously by all of these defendants up here, in particular, by a young man named Esad Landzo, who is facing the possibility of life imprisonment. It's a shame that the Prosecution put these accusations in a light of calling them a myth, that the Defence was a myth or a joke. We are not here to create myths. We're not here to create jokes. We're here as the embodiment of the aims and goals of the United Nations to see that justice is done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think this is the last of your submissions and we're very grateful for your efforts in lucidly stating in what perhaps might have been obscured in our earlier arguments. We are grateful you could find time within the limited period to put them down so succinctly that the Trial Chamber can be better guided in determining the evidence which has been put forward before us for the past -- how many months? About 18 or 19 months. It's a long time. We are grateful, perhaps, even if memory was failing. You have done enough to remind us of what has transpired, even for things that were out of the records because in your submissions so many things have been said, which perhaps may not be found in the record of proceedings themselves. We'll do our best as impartial arbiters between contesting parties. We're all familiar with justice in the way it has been done. We are particularly grateful to the parties and especially the Defence in the manner in which they have actually led evidence and trying to go to the root of the matter, even for areas we did not need to do so. So we're very grateful. As I said, we'll do our best in the interpretation of the provisions which are a little obscure in the views which have been severely criticised on both sides and in those areas where, perhaps, good jurisprudence allows a Trial Chamber to go to the bottom of the matter and determine issues as we see them. As you know, it takes some time to put these things down, to reflect on them and come out with a rational justice. I delicately use the word rational justice because of the issues confronting us and the situations under which we have been working. Thank you very much. This is the end of the open session, so it will be closed session when we next come around. It will be about reading the judgement and then of subsequent matters. You remember we promised you that we would not allow the amendment of the rules to prejudice your chances of bringing forward further evidence in the interest of plans of accused persons who have to produce evidence in mitigation of sentence. So we'll take that into consideration. And, if it becomes necessary to do that, we'll give you sufficient time to file such evidence or produce any such witnesses who might give testimony in respect of sentencing. Thank you very much. So we'll now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: 12.25 p.m., to be reconvened sine die.
